characterList.description: A white male, with short brown hair, wearing a grey shirt, a headset and sitting on a chair. A cat can be seen on the floor behind him
characterList.name: Jim Caffey

content_metadata.description: A scientific video series hosted by Professor Jim Caffey that takes viewers on a journey through space, exploring galaxies, planets, and other astronomical concepts.

qAndA.answer: The iron oxide, which is rust, is very prevalent on the surface of Mars, and that's what makes it look red.
qAndA.question: What makes Mars look red?

qAndA.answer: When galaxies collide they don't really crash like cars do, they kind of merge into a morph of each other.
qAndA.question: Why does Professor Caffey refer to galaxies as 'morphs'?

qAndA.answer: When a massive star explodes and dies the heavy elements formed inside that star are spread out into the Universe. Some of those heavy elements, like calcium and iron are what make up our bones and our blood.
qAndA.question: What is the relationship between a stellar corpse and the elements in our body?

qAndA.answer: City lights create light pollution, making it hard to see faint objects in the night sky, like the Milky Way.
qAndA.question: Why is it hard to see the Milky Way from a city?

qAndA.answer: It takes time for light to travel through space, so the farther away an object is, the longer it takes for its light to reach us. When we look at distant objects, we are seeing them as they were in the past. This concept is known as lookback time. In Astronomy, looking at very distant objects allows us to 'look back in time' and see how the Universe used to be.
qAndA.question: What is lookback time and why is it relevant in Astronomy?

narrativeProgression.description: Intro video starts with an animation showing planets Saturn and Jupiter and the Sun.
The animation shows a transition from Planet Saturn to Planet Earth.
Contact details for Professor Jim Caffey are shown on an orange background.
The title screen shows information about the episode, chapter, topics covered and two pictures, one showing a comet and another showing a telescope.

activities.description: Drawing an ellipse on the image of Mars
Drawing a circle on the image of Crab Nebula

scenes.contextualRelevance: Professor Caffey introduces the concept of galaxies and gives examples like NGC 1073, Andromeda, Milky Way, and Magellanic Clouds. He discusses planets in our Solar System and some dwarf planets like Pluto and Ceres. Telescopes like the Hubble and radio telescopes used to observe galaxies are introduced.

narrativeProgression.description: Professor Jim Caffey starts a tour of the Universe by presenting pictures of galaxies and planets.
The tour continues with pictures of the red planet Mars and the Valles Marineris.
The tour continues with a picture of a Stellar Corpse.
Professor Jim Caffey explains what a stellar corpse is and that the one in the picture is the Crab Nebula.
The tour continues with a picture of the Orion Nebula, a star birthing region.
The tour continues with a picture of the Hubble Telescope and the Earth.
The tour continues with a picture of Planet Earth, taken from a geostationary satellite.
The tour continues with a picture of the Earth and the Moon to scale.
The tour continues with a picture of our Solar Family, with all planets and dwarf planets.
The tour continues with a picture of a Spiral Galaxy called NGC 1073, thought to be similar to the Milky Way Galaxy.
The tour continues with a time lapse image of the Milky Way Galaxy.
The tour continues with a picture of a group of radio telescopes used to observe the Large Magellanic Cloud and the Small Magellanic Cloud, two minor galaxies close to us.
The tour continues with a picture of the Andromeda galaxy, the closest spiral galaxy to our Milky Way.
The tour continues with a picture of the Fornax Cluster of Galaxies.
The tour ends with a calendar showing a timeline of events in the Universe.

trimmingSuggestions.description: The intro video could be shortened, as the long fades between different objects decrease the dynamism of the segment.
The outro could also be trimmed to make it snappier, for example by removing the text overlay and simply having Professor Caffey deliver his message verbally while pointing to the Subscribe button.

Prof. Jim Caffey Presents: "10-Minute Astronomy!" 2021 Edition 

Award-Winning Online Astronomy Professor Jim Caffey, based in Springfield, Missouri, brings you "10-Minute Astronomy!" 2021 Edition, his new Lecture Video Series based on the FREE Text from OpenStax Astronomy. 

30 lectures and 15 short introductions were added and updated for 2021 with accurate close captions for the deaf and hearing impaired by Hidy Hesham (Cairo University, Giza, Egypt). Professor Caffey was named one of the Leading Online Astronomy Professors using Virtual and Immersive Technologies in 2008 by his peers in Astronomy Education. 

This lecture series is an OER - Open Educational Resource, meaning it can be shared and used freely, with credit given to Professor Jim Caffey. Designed for non-science majors, high school students, amateur and backyard astronomers, or the public. 

Welcome to "10-Minute Astronomy!" 2021 Edition!
